chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya and Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, both from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from Abbad ibn Yaqoub, from Ahmad ibn Ismail, from Amr ibn Kaysan, from Abu Abdillah Al-Ju'fy, who said:

Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him) said to me: 'How many Ribaat (guards) are there in your presence?' I said, 'Forty.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'But our Ribaat is the Ribaat of eternity. And whoever attaches an animal for us, he will have its weight, and the weight of its weight, as long as it is with him. And whoever attaches a weapon for us, he will have its weight, as long as it is with him.'
Do not grieve from once, or twice, or three times, or four, for our example and your example is like the example of a Prophet who was among the Children of Israel.
So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him: 'Call your people to the fighting, for I will help you.'

So he gathered them from the tops of the mountains and from other places, then he directed them. So they neither struck with their swords, nor did they stab with their spears, until they were defeated.
Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'Call your people to the fighting, for I will help you.'
So he called them. They said, 'You promised us the help, but no help came to us'.
So Allah the Exalted revealed to him: 'Either they choose the fighting or the Fire.'

So he said: 'O Lord! The fighting is more beloved to me than the Fire.' So he called them, and three hundred and thirteen of them answered him, the same number of the people of Badr. So he directed them. They neither struck with their swords, nor stabbed with their spears, until Allah, Mighty and Majestic, granted victory to them.

key_terms.أَهْلِ بَدْرٍ: People of Badr (referring to the companions of the Prophet Muhammad at the Battle of Badr)
key_terms.الرِّبَاطُ: Ribaat (guarding/staying in readiness for battle or religious duty)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for Ribaat (guarding) in the Shia tradition?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Baqir (as), the concept of Ribaat is elevated from a temporary military duty to an eternal spiritual state, with rewards tied to the weight of one's horse or weapon as long as they are kept ready. The Imam illustrates this through the story of a Prophet from Bani Israel who faced repeated delays in divine victory, teaching that patience through multiple trials ('not from once, nor twice, nor thrice') is essential. This narrative underscores the Shia principle that steadfastness in readiness for the Imam's cause yields immense, enduring reward regardless of immediate visible success.
